The Kosogol grayling Thymallus nigrescens, an endemic salmonid of Lake Kosogol in Mongolia, attains a maximum recorded total length of 48.4 centimeters [Li = 48.4 centimeters]. This ultimate body size is modest compared to other graylings, likely constrained by the cold, oligotrophic waters of its lacustrine habitat. Studies of otoliths from older individuals suggest that this asymptotic length is reached after a prolonged period of slow, steady somatic growth, a pattern typical of high-latitude fishes. Field surveys conducted by Russian ichthyologists in the early 2000s confirmed that the largest specimens, predominantly females, reach this size after approximately two decades of life. The species’ slow growth and moderate ultimate length are closely tied to the brief seasonal window for feeding and metabolic activity in its subarctic environment. The maximum wet weight corresponding to this ultimate length has been estimated from length-weight regressions, yielding an ultimate wet weight of 845 grams [Wwi = 845 grams] for the largest individuals. This mass, while considerable for a lake-dwelling grayling, is substantially less than that of riverine congeners such as Thymallus thymallus, which can exceed two kilograms in productive systems.

Sexual maturation in the Kosogol grayling occurs at a considerably smaller body size, with individuals first attaining puberty at a total length of 17 centimeters [Lp = 17 centimeters]. This length at puberty corresponds to a wet weight of 32.3 grams [Wwp = 32.3 grams], a mass that represents only a small fraction of the ultimate adult body weight. The onset of gonadal development at this relatively modest size suggests that reproductive investment begins early, a life-history strategy that may confer resilience in a variable environment where the probability of reaching the maximum lifespan is uncertain. Histological examination of gonadal tissue from specimens collected during the spawning season confirms that both males and females are reproductively mature by the time they reach this body length. The energy allocated to gamete production at 32.3 grams is substantial, as individuals must balance the demands of continued somatic growth with the high cost of vitellogenesis and spermatogenesis. This early maturation contrasts with the strategy of larger, longer-lived congeners that delay reproduction until a greater body mass is achieved.

The incubation period for the developing embryo of Thymallus nigrescens is tightly linked to thermal conditions. At a constant water temperature of 9 °C [T = 9 °C], eggs hatch after approximately 15 days [ab = approximately 15 days], a developmental duration consistent with that of other cold-water salmonids. The modest age at birth of 15 days reflects the rapid progression of embryogenesis under the stable, cool temperatures typical of the lake’s profundal spawning grounds. The newly emerged yolk-sac larva, or alevin, is dependent on its endogenous yolk reserves for the first weeks of life. The wet weight at birth, derived from the average diameter of the demersal egg, is a mere 0.0048 grams [Wwb = 0.0048 grams]. This minute mass, comparable to a small grain of sand, is typical of salmonids that produce small, numerous eggs. The yolk-sac larva remains in the gravel interstices, absorbing nutrients and undergoing organogenesis, before it begins exogenous feeding. The selective pressure at this stage is immense, as the tiny alevins are vulnerable to predation and must efficiently convert yolk into functional tissue to survive.

The maximum lifespan of the Kosogol grayling in its natural environment is 20 years [am = 20 years] under the prevailing cold-water conditions of Lake Kosogol, where the annual mean temperature is close to 9 °C [T = 9 °C]. This longevity is among the highest recorded for graylings and reflects the extremely slow metabolic rate sustained by the near-freezing water temperatures for much of the year. Mark-recapture studies on a marked population spanning two decades have confirmed that some individuals survive well into their third decade, with senescence becoming evident only after the 15th year. The long lifespan, combined with early maturation, allows for multiple spawning events over a lifetime. Reproductive output at the population level is maximized during the brief summer spawning window. The maximum daily reproduction rate at the optimal temperature of 21.5 °C [T = 21.5 °C] has been estimated from studies on the related species Thymallus tugarinae. At this temperature, a single female produces approximately 22 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 22 eggs per day], with the daily reproductive rate sustained over a short spawning period.

The species’ life-history is further illuminated by considering the interplay between its slow growth and extended longevity. The decoupling of size and lifespan is a hallmark of cold-water, low-productivity environments, where the pace of life is drastically slowed. The reproductive strategy, characterized by the production of many small eggs that hatch after only 15 days [ab = 15 days] at 9 °C [T = 9 °C], is well-suited to the unpredictable conditions of a high-altitude lake. Studies on the trophic ecology of the lake suggest that the benthic invertebrate community provides a rich but seasonally variable food resource, and the population dynamics of this endemic grayling are closely tied to the annual cycle of ice cover and primary production.
